title: What a dental practice manager does
meta_description: A plain guide to the dental practice manager role: core duties, a weekly routine, KPIs worth tracking and which front-desk tasks to automate first.
h1: What a dental practice manager does, and which tasks to automate
dek: The role covers people, money, compliance and patient flow. Here is how it fits together, a weekly routine, and what to hand to software.
key_takeaways: A practice manager runs the business side of a dental practice: people, money, compliance and patient flow.
Write the week down: roster Monday, money Tuesday, compliance Wednesday, patients Thursday, numbers Friday.
Track a few practice-defined numbers: no-shows, missed calls, recalls, unbooked treatment plans and new patient sources.
Automate repetitive messages first; keep fee talks, complaints and clinical judgement with people.
How online bookings reach the diary depends on your practice software setup, so check before automating.
body_html:
A practice manager runs the business side of a dental practice: the roster, the accounts, the compliance paperwork, the patient flow through the chairs, and the front desk that ties it all together. The dentists own the clinical care; the practice manager makes sure there is a functioning practice around it. Jobs and Skills Australia counts the role as its own occupation, with about 30,600 people working as practice managers across Australia, so it is worth being deliberate about how the job is set up rather than letting it grow by accident.

This guide sets out what the role covers, a weekly routine you can adapt, the numbers worth tracking, and which front-desk tasks are reasonable to hand to software first — with the judgement-heavy work kept with people. It is written for principals and practice managers working in dental practices, and much of it applies to medical and allied clinics too.

What does a dental practice manager actually do?

The official occupation description covers practice managers who organise and control the functions and resources of professional practices — the administrative systems and the practice personnel. In a dental practice that translates into five overlapping areas:

  • People. Hiring, rosters, training, performance reviews and the day-to-day coordination of reception, dental assistants and hygienists.
  • Money. Managing the records and accounts of the practice, patient payments, health fund questions and outstanding balances.
  • Compliance. Making sure work complies with relevant legislation, policies and procedures, and keeping the paperwork current.
  • Patients. Patient relations, complaints, recalls and the whole experience of contacting and visiting the practice.
  • Systems. The practice software, phones, booking tools and reports that everything runs through.

A sample job description from the American Dental Association describes the same territory for an office manager: day-to-day operations, staff assignments and schedules, patient financial accounts, patient relations, and managing and updating the office computer systems. Titles vary — some practices say office manager or business manager — but the mix is much the same.

The role is common enough to have its own employment profile. Within the practice manager group, health practice managers specifically number about 22,800 workers, and the role skews part-time: around 42% work part-time hours, which tells you the job is often combined with another role or shared between two people. Employers clearly keep hiring for it — the ADA Career Center listed 100 practice manager roles when we checked in November 2026.

30,600People employed as practice managers in AustraliaJobs and Skills Australia
$1,655Median weekly earnings before tax, practice managers overallJobs and Skills Australia
100Practice manager roles listed on the ADA Career CenterChecked 12 Nov 2026

Two of these areas are easy to underestimate. The money side is not just banking: it includes quoting and explaining fees before treatment, keeping track of treatment that has been planned but not started, following up outstanding balances without souring the relationship, and answering the health fund questions that arrive several times a day. The compliance side is mostly invisible when it is done well — current policies, staff certifications, equipment registers, privacy and record-keeping habits — and expensive when it is not. Neither area produces applause, which is exactly why both belong on a written routine rather than in someone's memory.

One person, or three hats on one head?

Not every practice can justify a dedicated, full-time manager, and the employment data reflects that: a large share of health practice managers work part-time hours. In small practices the role is often assembled from overlapping jobs — a senior receptionist who also does rosters and accounts, an owner dentist who handles compliance and hiring, and a bookkeeper who takes the financial reports. That arrangement can work well, but it fails in predictable ways: two people each assume the other sent the reminder, nobody owns the recall list, and decisions stall because no one is sure who decides.

If the role is shared, write the split down. A one-page map — who owns roster, money, compliance, patient experience and systems, and who decides when they conflict — costs an hour and prevents the "I thought you were doing it" conversations that erode a front desk. Revisit it whenever staff change, because the split that worked with three people rarely survives down to two.

A week that works, written down

Because the role spans so many areas, the difference between a controlled week and a chaotic one is usually a written routine. Each weekday gets a theme, and everything that is not urgent gets parked to its day rather than interrupting something else. Adapt the shape below to your opening hours, staff meetings and school-holiday patterns.

  1. Monday Check the roster and the diary for the fortnight ahead; confirm cover before the week fills up.
  2. Tuesday Money day: outstanding accounts, unpaid treatment plans, health fund queries and payment follow-ups.
  3. Wednesday One compliance or HR item: policies, certifications, training records, equipment registers.
  4. Thursday Patients: the recall list, patients who accepted a plan but have not booked, and review requests.
  5. Friday Numbers: the week's calls, no-shows and bookings, then set Monday's priorities before you leave.

The themes are examples rather than rules. The point is that roster questions, accounts questions and patient questions each get a predictable slot, so the day is not decided entirely by whoever calls loudest. A monthly item — supplier reviews, marketing planning, a full numbers review — can sit on the same weekday each month so it is never "when there is time".

Where the front-desk time actually goes

Ask any practice manager where the pressure lands and the answer is usually the phone and the diary: missed calls during chairside hours, reminder follow-ups, patients wanting to move bookings, and chasing people who said yes to treatment and then went quiet. The ADA sample job description assumes the office manager will "help support staff as needed" with appointment scheduling and collections — in a small practice, that support is most of the job. Missed calls deserve particular attention, because each one is an enquiry that may never have reached the desk; we wrote separately about what happens when a patient does not show up, and the same respectful follow-up thinking applies to calls that went unanswered.

After-hours is the sharpest version of the problem. A dental practice that closes at 5 pm still receives calls in the evening: parents ringing about a chipped tooth, patients running late who want to warn the practice, new patients who could only look up clinics after work. An office phone that rings out after hours sends those people to the next search result. Whether a practice answers those calls with a person, an after-hours service or an AI voice receptionist, the important part is that something takes a message, records the caller's details and makes the next step obvious for the morning team. Set expectations carefully in the after-hours message itself: the practice is not open, emergencies belong with 000 or an emergency department, and anything non-urgent will be picked up when the desk reopens.

The trap in automating is applying software to the wrong half of the job. Communication that is repetitive, timely and templated suits software well. Judgement does not. The split below is a fair starting point for a dental front desk.

Hand to software

  • After-hours and overflow calls, answered with a message taken
  • Missed-call text-back and appointment reminder sequences
  • Follow-up with patients who accepted a plan but have not booked
  • Review requests after completed visits
  • Booking links, confirmations and routine questions like location and parking

Keep human

  • Fee conversations and payment arrangements
  • Complaints, and patients who sound anxious or upset
  • Clinical questions — the clinician decides
  • Exceptions: which fee applies to whom, and when to waive it
  • Anything a patient clearly wants to discuss with a person

Start with messages, not decisions

The safest place to begin is the communication a practice repeats dozens of times a week: reminders, confirmations, reschedule replies and text-backs after a missed call. These follow a pattern you can write once, reuse, and steadily improve. An example rebooking thread:

Example reminder and rebooking thread

Hi [First name], this is [Practice]. You have a check-up with Dr Lee on Tue 10 Nov at 9:20 am. Reply 1 to confirm or 2 to rebook.

9:41 AM

2 please — Thursday afternoon works better for me

11:02 AM

No problem, we can move it. We have Thu 12 Nov at 2:40 pm or Fri 13 Nov at 9:00 am. Which suits?

11:04 AM

Thursday is good

11:20 AM

Templates like this are a starting point: keep the practice name, use the patient's preferred name and channel, and keep the wording plain. A reminder that is only a reminder is different from a marketing message — but the moment an offer or promotion is added, the ACMA's spam rules require consent, sender identification and a working unsubscribe. This guide is general information, not legal advice.

Automation also needs a handover. If a text conversation goes beyond the template — an unusual request, a complaint, an emergency — someone must pick it up quickly, and patients should be able to reach a human in one step. Write the handover rule down before the first automated message goes out.

  1. CaptureUnanswered calls get an automatic text-back attempt.
  2. ReplyThe patient's question is answered or a link is sent.
  3. BookThe patient chooses a time from the online booking link.
  4. Hand overAnything beyond the template goes to a person the same day.

The numbers worth tracking

You do not need a dashboard for everything. A handful of practice-defined measures, reviewed weekly in the Friday slot, are enough to steer the roster, the diary and the follow-up list. Definitions matter more than benchmarks: compare against your own last month, not against another practice, and write each definition down so the number means the same thing next quarter.

MeasureWhat it tells youWhere it usually lives
No-shows and late cancellationsWhether reminders and the booking mix are workingDiary report
Missed callsEnquiries that may never have reached the deskPhone or call log
Recall rebooking rateHow well due patients are returningRecall list
Unbooked treatment plansPatients who accepted a plan but have not bookedTreatment tracker
New patient sourcesWhere enquiries come from, so you can back the ones that workSource tracking

Two of these connect to work we have written about before: source tracking is what makes lead management more than a spreadsheet, and the no-show figure only becomes useful once your practice decides how it responds — see what we suggest measuring and the follow-up wording for patients who miss a visit.

Run the review the same way every week: look at last week against the same measure a week earlier, note anything that moved by more than usual, and pick at most one action. A single change — moving reminder timing, adding a text-back to the after-hours message, calling the five oldest unbooked treatment plans — is something you can actually attribute. A list of five actions tells you nothing about what worked.

Questions to ask before you automate

Before switching anything on, work through the checklist with the person who will own it. The answers decide how well the automation lands with patients and staff, and several of them are about people rather than software.

  • Which messages are repetitive enough to template today?
  • Who reviews exceptions — and can they waive a fee or rebook without escalating?
  • What happens to an after-hours call, and who checks the messages each morning?
  • How do online bookings reach the diary, and what does that depend on in your practice software setup?
  • Can a patient reach a human in one step when the template does not fit?
  • Which consent and opt-out wording applies to each message type?
  • Who owns each weekly number, and when is it reviewed?

Bringing the front desk with you

Whichever tasks move to software, the reception team hears about the change before patients do. The pattern that works is boring and effective: explain what the tool takes over and what it does not, agree who reviews its messages each day, and keep the human handover path obvious. Staff who fear being replaced will quietly route around a new system; staff who are told the phone overflow is now handled so they can stay with the patient in front of them will usually defend it. Celebrate the boring wins out loud — the Tuesday when nobody had to stay late chasing unpaid accounts — because that is what makes the next change easier.

Where DrKing fits

DrKing is an AI front desk for Australian clinics: one inbox for web chat, phone, SMS, email and social messages, an AI voice receptionist that answers and takes messages, missed-call text-back, online booking, appointment reminders, review requests, text-to-pay, source tracking and monthly database reactivation. It also follows up patients who accepted a treatment plan but have not booked, and plans SMS and email campaigns, including a 12-month calendar. Records stay in your practice software — DrKing works alongside it, depending on your setup. See how this looks for dental practices on the dental hub.

faq.q: What is the difference between a dental practice manager and an office manager?
faq.a: Titles vary between practices and overlap heavily. Both usually cover day-to-day operations, staff coordination, patient accounts and the systems the practice runs on; the American Dental Association sample job description uses office manager for the same territory. What matters is that one person owns the business side, and that staff and patients know which decisions that person can make.

faq.q: Do you need a qualification to work as a practice manager in Australia?
faq.a: Jobs and Skills Australia notes that formal qualifications are not essential for health practice managers, although some workers hold vocational or university qualifications in business, management, nursing, dental or clerical fields. Experience running a busy front desk, comfort with practice software and sound judgement about people matter most in the day-to-day work.

faq.q: Which tasks should a dental practice automate first?
faq.a: Start with repetitive, templated communication: appointment reminders, confirmations, missed-call text-back and follow-up with patients who accepted a treatment plan but have not booked. Keep fee discussions, complaints and clinical questions with people. Before switching anything on, check how online bookings reach your diary, because that depends on your practice software setup.

faq.q: How do you know if front-desk automation is working?
faq.a: Compare your practice-defined numbers before and after the change: missed calls, no-shows and late cancellations, recall rebooking rate and unbooked treatment plans. Definitions matter more than benchmarks, so review against your own previous weeks rather than figures from another practice, and keep each definition written down so it stays consistent.
